name: Antiperspirant

lead: Antiperspirants keep your underarms dry. That means no sweat marks on shirts, less of the moisture odor-causing bacteria feed on, and a fresher presence through the day.

Aluminium salts react with sweat and form temporary plugs in the sweat ducts, with a mild astringent effect, so less sweat reaches the skin surface. Sweat reduction is measurable, and stronger versions of the same ingredient family are used for excessive sweating. This differs from a deodorant, which targets odor rather than sweat output.

paras: Most people apply a stick, roll-on, spray or gel to clean, dry underarms as part of a daily grooming routine, and often pair it with a deodorant or fragrance. Stronger formulas exist for heavy sweaters. The effect builds with regular use.

Skin irritation is the most common effect, and zirconium-containing products can cause granulomas. The FDA advises people with kidney problems to consult a doctor first. Concerns about breast cancer and Alzheimer's have been studied, and reviews summarized on Wikipedia found no reliable link.

chain: Drier clothes, less odor, fresher presence
angle.text: Antiperspirants cut underarm sweat with aluminium salts, so shirts stay dry and the moisture odor bacteria feed on is reduced. It is the everyday staple of a grooming routine, and the sweat reduction is visible and measurable.

lead: An antiperspirant is a topical product that reduces sweating, most commonly using aluminium salts such as aluminium chlorohydrate or aluminium zirconium compounds. It differs from a deodorant, which targets underarm odor rather than sweat output, although many commercial sticks combine both functions.[1][2] In the United States products that contain an antiperspirant agent are regulated as over-the-counter drugs, while plain deodorants are cosmetics; in the European Union antiperspirants are generally treated as cosmetics.[1][2]

For appearance, the payoff is dry underarms and dry clothing: no visible sweat marks on shirts, less odor, and more confidence in formal, close-contact or photographed settings. A 2023 systematic review in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science describes antiperspirant technology as reducing sweat flow, which lowers odor and also improves a person's appearance.[3] Aluminium salts are thought to react with electrolytes in sweat to form temporary gel plugs in the sweat-duct openings, so less sweat reaches the skin surface.[1][3] The same ingredient family at higher strengths is the usual first-line topical approach for hyperhidrosis, or excessive sweating.[4][5]

The commercial history runs from Mum, patented in 1888, and Everdry, sold from 1903, through Jules Montenier's 1941 formulation, the 1952 roll-on and the aerosols of the 1960s.[1] Research on antiperspirants is dominated by safety questions that became popular on the internet and in forums: whether aluminium contributes to breast cancer or Alzheimer's disease. The National Cancer Institute states that no scientific evidence links antiperspirant use to breast cancer, and a 2024 meta-analysis of seven case-control studies found no association.[6][7] Related products include deodorants, alum crystal sticks, clinical-strength antiperspirants and, for severe cases, medical treatments for hyperhidrosis.[1][4]
infobox: Aluminium chlorohydrate; aluminium zirconium tetrachlorohydrex gly[1]
Cosmetic; SCCS 2020 opinion on aluminium limits[1]

paras: Antiperspirants come as sticks, roll-ons, aerosol and pump sprays, gels and creams, and are frequently sold combined with deodorant.[2] Aluminium chlorohydrate and aluminium zirconium compounds are the common actives in non-prescription products.[1] Alcohols, propylene glycol and fragrances are typical supporting ingredients.[1]

Wikipedia's coverage of the broader deodorant category separates three approaches: antiperspirants that reduce sweating, antibacterial deodorants that slow the bacteria that act on sweat, and masking products that cover odor with fragrance.[1] Stronger clinical-strength versions are sold for heavy sweating, and prescription-strength aluminium chloride solutions exist for hyperhidrosis.[2][4]

sections.h: How people use it to look better
paras: The underarm is where apocrine glands, which produce the oily protein- and lipid-rich sweat that bacteria turn into odor, are concentrated; apocrine glands become active at puberty, which is why odor usually starts then.[1] A 2015 Microbiome study mapped the underarm bacteria that produce body odors.[8] Antiperspirant users aim to cut both the wetness and the smell.

Wikipedia notes that antiperspirants are generally most effective when applied at bedtime, when sweating is low, allowing the active to enter the ducts and form plugs before the skin becomes active again.[1] The plugs are lost as the skin renews, so regular reapplication is needed.[1]

A recurring appearance issue is clothing: aluminium zirconium tetrachlorohydrex gly can react with sweat and leave yellow marks on fabric, and underarm liners are described as a way to avoid staining.[1] Men's grooming and strength-training communities discuss antiperspirant mainly in terms of pit stains, gym and competition use; one T Nation poster describes still looking for a dependable antiperspirant for powerlifting meets because of heavy sweating.[9]

Edna Murphey patented a deodorant cream, Mum, in 1888 in Philadelphia, and Bristol-Myers bought the company in 1931.[1] Everdry, introduced in 1903, is cited as the first commercial antiperspirant.[1] Aluminium chloride products were irritating to skin and fabric; on 28 January 1941 Jules Montenier patented a formulation that reduced this irritation, first sold as Stopette spray and promoted through the television quiz show What's My Line?.[1]

Helen Barnett Diserens developed an applicator modelled on the ballpoint pen in the late 1940s, which was marketed as Ban Roll-On in 1952.[1] Between 1942 and 1957 the deodorant market grew roughly 600-fold, to about 70 million dollars, and marketing widened from women to men; by 1957 an estimated half of men used deodorant.[1]

Gillette's Right Guard became the first aerosol antiperspirant in the early 1960s, and aerosols reached about 82 percent of antiperspirant sales by the early 1970s.[1] In 1977 the US Food and Drug Administration banned an aluminium zirconium aerosol ingredient over inhalation concerns, and restrictions on CFC propellants also contributed to the rise of stick products.[1] Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, also describes earlier alum-based products, but those details are less reliable.[2]

Eccrine glands over most of the body produce a watery, largely odorless sweat, while apocrine glands in the armpits and groin produce a thicker secretion that skin bacteria metabolise into odor compounds.[1] Aluminium salts are described as reacting with electrolytes in sweat to form gel plugs in the ducts and binding to keratin there, with a mild astringent effect at the pore opening.[1][3]

Alum crystal sticks, marketed as natural deodorants, contain aluminium in a different chemical form than antiperspirant salts and act chiefly by inhibiting bacteria; they can be weak irritants.[1] Other deodorant approaches include antimicrobials, pH-adjusting products and activated charcoal, and methenamine has been studied as a strong antiperspirant for sweating in prosthetic sockets.[1]

Clinical-strength antiperspirants contain higher concentrations of aluminium chloride and are used for hyperhidrosis. Wikipedia's hyperhidrosis article describes topical aluminium products as the first-line therapy, with improvement taking a few days and skin irritation as the most common side effect.[4] A 2025 review in Internal Medicine Journal outlines the wider range of options for focal and generalised sweating.[5]

Beyond topicals, Wikipedia lists oral anticholinergic drugs, a topical anticholinergic approved by the FDA in 2018 for primary underarm sweating, tap-water iontophoresis, botulinum toxin injections that last roughly three to nine months, and surgical options such as sweat-gland removal or sympathectomy.[4] Focal hyperhidrosis may affect up to about 2.8 percent of the US population.[4]

A 2022 randomized trial in the Journal der Deutschen Dermatologischen Gesellschaft enrolled 50 participants with excessive underarm and groin sweating to compare an aluminium lactate-based antiperspirant with an aluminium chloride-based one.[10]

Breast cancer: the belief that underarm products cause breast cancer is described by Wikipedia as originating in a 1999 chain email.[1] The National Cancer Institute says no scientific evidence links antiperspirant or deodorant use to breast cancer. It cites a 2002 study by Mirick, Davis and Thomas of 813 women with breast cancer and 793 without, which found no increased risk, and notes that a 2003 retrospective study by McGrath of 437 survivors linked frequent use with younger age at diagnosis, a result the institute calls inconclusive because of its design.[6][11][12] A 2024 meta-analysis of seven case-control studies reported an odds ratio of 0.96 (95 percent confidence interval 0.78 to 1.17) and called for prospective cohort studies.[7]

Researchers who argue for further investigation include authors of a 2016 review in Morphologie, who point to higher aluminium levels measured in breast tissue and fluids than in blood and to the upper outer quadrant, near the underarm, being the site of a disproportionate share of breast cysts and cancers.[13] A 2024 review in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences discusses aluminium as a possible metalloestrogen while noting that regulators at the stated antiperspirant concentrations do not classify it as carcinogenic.[14] Wikipedia attributes the higher cancer incidence near the armpit to the distribution of breast tissue, including the tail of Spence.[1]

Alzheimer's disease: a 1990 epidemiological study and a prospective analysis from the Canadian Study of Health and Aging examined aluminium-containing products and dementia and reported differing findings.[15][16] A 2014 review of 469 studies cited by Wikipedia found little evidence that aluminium salt exposure increases risk.[1] A toxicokinetics review describes food as the primary common source of aluminium exposure.[17] A 2020 experimental study in Skin Pharmacology and Physiology followed 21 healthy people to examine how daily antiperspirant use affects systemic aluminium load.[18]

Skin and other effects: zirconium can trigger an allergic axillary granuloma, propylene glycol can irritate or sensitise skin, and alum crystals are weak irritants.[1] The FDA advises people with kidney dysfunction to consult a doctor before using aluminium antiperspirants, since they may absorb more aluminium. Aerosols held close to the skin can cause frostbite-like burns.[1] Axillary granular parakeratosis is a described underarm skin condition.[19]

In the US, products containing antiperspirant agents are regulated as over-the-counter drugs, while deodorants without such agents are cosmetics.[1] Wikipedia reports that the FDA said in 2003 that available data were not sufficient to change the status of aluminium antiperspirants.[1] In the EU the Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety could not complete a risk assessment in 2015 because of insufficient dermal data, and in 2020 considered aluminium compounds safe up to 6.25 percent in non-spray products and 10.60 percent in sprays.[1]

Epidemiological work on antiperspirant use and breast cancer includes the 2002 Journal of the National Cancer Institute case-control study, a 2003 retrospective study on age at diagnosis, and the 2024 meta-analysis of seven case-control studies.[11][12][7] Alzheimer's research is observational and includes a 1990 case-control study and the Canadian Study of Health and Aging.[15][16] Efficacy work includes a randomized trial of two antiperspirant formulations in 50 participants.[10] Findings in the epidemiological literature differ in direction between early and later studies, and the studies are observational.

lore.intro: Antiperspirant comes up in men's grooming and lifting forums mostly in two ways: practical talk about stains, gym use and heavy sweating, and recurring worries about aluminium.[20][21][22][9]

timeline.event: Edna Murphey patents Mum, an underarm deodorant cream, in Philadelphia.[1]
Everdry is marketed as the first commercial antiperspirant.[1]
Jules Montenier patents a less irritating aluminium antiperspirant formulation, first used in Stopette.[1]
Ban Roll-On, based on Helen Barnett Diserens's ballpoint-style applicator, is launched.[1]
Gillette's Right Guard becomes the first aerosol antiperspirant.[1]
FDA bans an aluminium zirconium aerosol ingredient over inhalation concerns.[1]
A chain email links underarm products to breast cancer, according to Wikipedia.[1]
Journal of the National Cancer Institute case-control study of antiperspirant use and breast cancer is published.[11]
EU scientific committee cannot complete an aluminium risk assessment for lack of dermal data.[1]
FDA approves a topical anticholinergic for primary underarm sweating.[4]
EU committee considers aluminium compounds safe up to stated limits in non-spray and spray products.[1]
Meta-analysis of seven case-control studies reports no association with breast cancer.[7]
